title: Your First Program
description: Every word in a Java program explained, line by line, so none of it is magic.

content.value: Here is a complete Java program. It prints one line. Every other program you write this year starts from this shape, so it is worth taking apart properly.

`public class Main {` starts the class. A class is a named container for code, and this one is called `Main`. `public` means anything is allowed to use it. The `{` opens the container; the last `}` in the file closes it.

`public static void main(String[] args) {` starts the method named `main`. This name is special: when the JVM starts your program it looks for `main` and begins there. Get the name wrong and your program compiles but refuses to start, because nothing told the JVM where to begin.

The other words on that line each have a job. `static` means the method belongs to the class itself, so the JVM can call it without building anything first. `void` means the method hands nothing back when it finishes. `String[] args` is a place for words typed on the command line; you will not need it for a while, but `main` must have it.

`System.out.println("Hello, world!");` is the one real instruction. `System.out` is the screen, `println` means "print this, then move to a new line", and the text in double quotes is what gets printed. The semicolon ends the instruction.
Read `System.out.println` as a path: in the `System`, find its `out` (the screen), and tell it to `println`. Java is full of these dotted paths, and they always read left to right like that.

Java insists that a file holding a `public class Main` is named `Main.java`. The name in the code and the name of the file have to match, letter for letter, including capitals. Rename the class and you must rename the file too.

In this editor the file is already called `Main.java`, so keep your class named `Main` and you never have to think about it. If you do rename the class, the compiler will tell you at once, which is Java being strict on your behalf again.

Every `{` needs a matching `}`. The class opens one pair and the method opens another inside it, so a one-line program still ends with two closing braces. The indentation, those four spaces before each inner line, is not required by Java but it shows the nesting at a glance and every Java programmer uses it.
Try it in the editor. Add a third `System.out.println` of your own between the existing ones and run it: your line appears exactly where you put it, because instructions run top to bottom.

practice.question: Print your own name on one line, then your favourite food on a second line. Two instructions inside `main`.
Print a three line message: Java is strict. / Braces come in pairs. / And I am fine with that. Each on its own line.

quiz.question: Where does the JVM start running your program?
options: At the first line of the file.
quiz.explain: The JVM looks for `main` by name and starts there. That is why the spelling of `main` matters so much.

quiz.question: Your class is `public class Player`. What must the file be called?
quiz.explain: The file name must match the public class exactly, capitals included. `Player` goes in `Player.java`.

quiz.question: What does `println` do that plain printing would not?
options: It moves to a new line after printing.
It prints in a larger size.
quiz.explain: The `ln` stands for line: it prints your text and then starts a new line, so the next output appears underneath.

quiz.question: How many closing braces does the smallest program need?
options: Two: one for the method and one for the class.
None, if the program is short enough.
quiz.explain: Each `{` needs its own `}`. The class opens one and the method opens another, so two must be closed.
